name: Lena Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, parties or AI firms. Your answers are confidential. Lena, what is a usual day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look up old faults with AI before the van leaves, check the dated drawing and then spend most of the shift isolating and repairing overhead lines. I like the moment a meter reading finally explains a hot joint. I dislike a parts list that looks perfect on a screen but sends us to the wrong cabinet while the children wait for supper.

say: I would praise **faster fault lookup** while keeping physical checks with the crew.
I would teach the apprentice to verify the **dated drawing**.
think: I expect **regular wages** and line repairs to continue.
Our **four-month cushion** keeps school plans independent of the next callout.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and check AI results against dated drawings.
Show the apprentice how to spot an **old revision** in search results.
feel: I feel **comfortable** with a small improvement to the day.
S0.quote: AI can find a cable diagram, but it cannot smell burned insulation in a cabinet.
fieldNote: Lena uses **AI lookup daily** and remembers a renumbered feeder where the dated drawing prevented a wrong cabinet opening.
Her **four-month reserve** and regular wage make the mild scenario feel secure rather than financially urgent.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and verify daily AI searches against dated drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the AI lookup I use every morning saves a walk to the archive cupboard, but the overhead line still needs us. I check the original drawing before the van leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am glad the tools stay modest in this picture. We have about four months of expenses saved and the regular wage covers the mortgage, so the children's school plans do not depend on the next callout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the line roster and use AI to find earlier fault records, then check the dated drawing against the pole number. In the first year I would show the new apprentice how to spot an old revision in the search results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable. The faster lookup might mean I get home before the children finish supper, and that is plenty of improvement for one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did an old revision matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A feeder near the sports hall was renumbered after a new pole went in. The search pulled up the older number, but the dated drawing kept us from opening the wrong cabinet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust the lookup to choose the repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the crew still has to test the line and inspect the damage. AI can find a cable diagram, but it cannot smell burned insulation in a cabinet.

say: I would support **parts-order trials** that show why a fitting was chosen.
I would ask for **repeat-trip counts** before schedules tighten.
think: I expect **buying jobs** to shrink before my physical line shifts.
I worry **paid safety checks** could be treated as wasted time.
do: Join the paid **parts-order pilot** and compare suggested with fitted parts.
Publish **repeat-trip evidence** with other crews and seek schedule corrections.
feel: I feel **interested and watchful** about field hours and office jobs.
S1.quote: A trial is only fair if the field hours and office jobs are both visible.
fieldNote: Lena volunteers for **early field testing** and wants a repeat-trip count, not just a tidy parts list.
She sees **office displacement** and field safety time as linked costs that should appear in the same review.

steps.text: Test AI parts orders against actual fittings on paid shifts
Combine repeat-trip records with other crews for a staff meeting
Continue paid line repair shifts during the pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot I would test a buying system if the crew can see why it chose a fitting. A neat parts list is useful only when the bracket on the pole matches the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and scheduling jobs may shrink first, while the line repairs stay with us for now. I worry a faster computer plan could make the company count our safety check as wasted time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for the first paid parts-order pilot and record each suggested part beside the part we actually fit. In its first year I would ask the supervisor to publish the repeat-trip count and adjust the schedule when the system sends us back to stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested, with one eye on the people at the buying desk. I like trying tools. A trial is only fair if the field hours and office jobs are both visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part would be hard to predict?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bracket behind the sports hall had corrosion under the paint, so the standard fitting would not sit flush. We only saw the problem after the cover came off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you involve colleagues beyond the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show two other crews the records and ask them to add their own examples. If the repeat trips grew, we would take the combined log to a staff meeting.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from physical line robots around 2031.
I would request a **dead-span trial** before robots make live repairs.
think: At **48**, field robots could reduce my physical repair hours.
Our **four-month cushion** buys decision time but cannot replace years of wages.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2029 and ask about funded electrical testing posts.
Take a **paid qualification** only if tied to an advertised field job.
feel: I feel **nervous and curious** about losing physical work.
S2.quote: My daily AI habit is useful for records, but it will not guarantee paid work once a machine can make the physical joint.
fieldNote: Lena does not confuse **AI fluency** with protection after robots reach hands-on repairs around 2031.
Her **field testing plan** requires a funded vacancy, site measurements and comparable pay before she risks the family cushion.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2028 can plan the repair, but robots doing physical line work arrive around 2031. I would ask to help test their first joints on a dead practice span.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the plan changes and 48 when robots can fit cable. Four months of savings gives us time to choose, but not enough to carry a mortgage and two children through a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a paid qualification in field electrical testing if a funded post is advertised. In 2029 I would keep paid line shifts, take the qualification if the job is real and apply for the post after comparing its wage with mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel nervous and curious together. My daily AI habit is useful for records, but it will not guarantee paid work once a machine can make the physical joint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would field electrical testing involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to inspect a finished connection at the site and measure whether it carries the load safely. If the job is only writing test reports, full AI could do that before robots even arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family do with the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the four-month fund for a genuine wage gap, not spend it on a speculative course. My partner would want to see the job advert before we change anything.

say: I would request **load-test records** from robot-made joints.
I would distinguish **2031 planning AI** from physical robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need full pay for the mortgage.
A **report-writing test job** may vanish under full AI.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2032 and inspect robot trial joints.
Apply for a **posted testing role** only with guaranteed field hours.
feel: I feel **less rushed** with time to measure real site work.
S3.quote: A joint near the water tower looked clean last month but heated under load.
fieldNote: Lena centers **load measurements**, using a recent hot joint as a concrete challenge for robot trial success claims.
She wants **guaranteed field hours** in any testing role, since full AI could write the reports.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and inspect trial joints in 2032
Apply for an advertised field testing role with guaranteed paid site hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years is enough to collect a useful record of failed robot joints. Full AI reaches planning in 2031, while physical robots reach the lines around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the office changes and 51 when robots arrive. My older child may be leaving school, but I could still owe on the mortgage and I cannot assume a testing job will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a paid trial place on the field testing crew and keep notes on repairs that look sound but fail under load. In 2032 I would keep line shifts, inspect trial joints and apply for an advertised testing post only if its field hours were guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than in the two-year picture. I can see which measurements still need a person at the site, rather than betting on a report-writing role AI might erase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the load, the weather and the reading from the test meter. A joint near the water tower looked clean last month but heated under load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach a robot crew from those notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the training was on paid time and the faults stayed in a shared record. I would want the safety lead to see the hot joint example before a trial was called successful.

say: I would seek **multi-winter robot records** and yearly field hours.
I would distinguish **2036 planning AI** from field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, grown children do not establish a paid mortgage or retirement income.
Our **four-month reserve** belongs to family emergencies, not a personal robot purchase.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2037 and review annual trial records.
Apply for a **funded field testing job** if crew hours fall and site work pays.
feel: I feel **steady now** and open to a proven field role.
S4.quote: A new title alone is not a reason to move.
fieldNote: Lena treats the decade as **paid physical work** and watches for repeat robot performance across winters.
She keeps the **existing reserve** for family emergencies and avoids treating a robot timetable as retirement funding.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs through 2037 and review yearly field hours
Apply for funded field testing work if crew hours decline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot a decade gives time to test machines through several winters. Full thinking AI changes plans around 2036, and line-capable robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the first date and 56 when robots arrive. My children may have their own homes, but that does not tell me the mortgage balance or whether retirement is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep repairing lines and request yearly records of field hours and failed robot joints. In 2037 I would continue paid shifts, compare those records with my partner and apply for a funded field testing vacancy if our crew hours were falling and the site work still paid well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years because the line still needs us. The decade gives me room to test a new field role without pretending that a robot date is a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put your savings into equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the utility owns the line equipment and I do not need a machine in my garage. I would leave our four-month reserve for family emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay on repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the crews still have paid work and the repair trials do not show a safe replacement, I would stay. I like the physical work. A new title alone is not a reason to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line-capable robots could arrive around 2031 while my children still depend on my wage. A paid field electrical testing qualification tied to an advertised post, honest robot joint results and comparable pay would help me decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a testing job still pays for site measurements after AI writes the reports. A certificate for a desk role could be worthless before the robots even arrive.

headlineQuote: A certificate for a desk role could be worthless before the robots even arrive.
portrait: Lena is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for fault records and checks dated drawings before field repairs.
Her **four-month reserve** and regular wage give time to assess new roles without gambling family money.
Across the scenarios she seeks **load-test evidence**, funded field training and guaranteed site hours.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves only about three years before robots could fit physical line joints.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **electrical testing qualification**, advertised field role and honest joint results would help her decide.
